query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated Q235 steel, the formation and integrity of its natural, thin iron oxide passivation layer dictate the onset of corrosion. At room temperature, this passive film remains relatively defect‐free and suppresses further corrosive degradation, whereas at elevated temperatures the increased ionic mobility and thermal activation promote defect formation and porosity in the oxide layer, leading to accelerated corrosion initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with a native, thin iron oxide layer formed from ambient conditions
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel samples to a corrosive chloride-rich electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under controlled conditions at two set temperatures (room temperature ~25°C and an elevated temperature, e.g., 60°C)
generation.conditions: Controlled humidity and electrolyte composition in a standardized test chamber; samples prepared with identical surface finishes and pre-exposure histories; exposure durations repeated over fixed intervals to capture early-stage corrosion phenomena
generation.structural_mediator: The quality—in particular the defect density and continuity—of the passive iron oxide film on the steel surface
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the slower kinetics favor a more uniform and intact oxide film that limits ion exchange and corrosion propagation. Elevated temperatures accelerate both the formation and breakdown processes; the increased thermal energy enhances the diffusion of corrosive species (e.g., Cl− ions) into the film and promotes defect generation (porosity, microcracks) in the passive layer, thereby lowering its protective capability and initiating localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline maintained at room temperature, samples exposed at elevated temperatures will exhibit significantly higher corrosion rates as evidenced by increased corrosion current densities, reduced polarization resistances, greater mass losses, and more pronounced pitting or surface degradation.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples maintained under identical corrosive conditions at room temperature (~25°C), serving as the untreated reference regarding corrosion progression
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for pre-exposed, untreated Q235 steel in chloride-rich environments under moderate temperature elevations (up to about 60°C) where thermally activated defect formation in the passive film is expected to dominate the corrosion mechanism; results may not extend to conditions with additional mechanical stresses or markedly different chemical environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative threshold where temperature-induced defect formation significantly compromises the passive film is uncertain, and additional environmental factors (e.g., pH variations, dissolved oxygen level) may interact with the temperature effect. Detailed thermal–electrochemical kinetics remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of identically finished Q235 steel samples with verified native oxide films. Divide the samples into two groups: one maintained at room temperature (~25°C) and the other at an elevated temperature (e.g., 60°C). Expose both groups to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution in well-controlled environmental chambers that regulate humidity and eliminate extraneous variables. Use replicate samples for statistical significance and run the experiments for several intervals (e.g., 24, 72, and 168 hours).
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current density (icorr)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to measure polarization resistance
Mass loss measurements to quantify accelerated corrosion
Surface imaging (SEM) to assess pitting, defect density, and morphological degradation of the passive film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature samples do not show statistically significant increases in corrosion current density, decreases in polarization resistance, greater mass loss, or more extensive pitting (and related defect features in the passive film) compared to the room temperature samples, then the hypothesis that temperature-induced defect formation in the passive film drives accelerated corrosion will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA were selected as the composition of coating because of its high strength and corrosion resistance in bulk state, while the corresponding properties of coating remain unknown. Therefore, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating on the Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by using the plasma spray technique, and the microstructure evolution during preparation process, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution were investigated. Furthermore, the phase formation and the corrosion behavior of the coatings were specifically analyzed.
